question: A junior risk analyst at a US public pension fund is drafting the glossary that will accompany the fund’s new delta-normal VaR report. A senior colleague asks her to keep only the entry that is fully consistent with the definitions used in the report’s methodology. Which of the following entries is most accurate?

options.A: Marginal VaR: the change in portfolio VaR from adding an entire new position, measured by computing the portfolio VaR before and after the trade.
options.B: Individual VaR: the VaR of a position in isolation, computed with the signed position, so that a short position carries a negative individual VaR.
options.C: Component VaR: a partition of portfolio VaR showing approximately how much portfolio VaR would change if the component were deleted; the components sum to portfolio VaR.
options.D: Undiversified VaR: the sum of the individual VaRs, which equals the portfolio VaR whenever all correlations are unity, whether or not any positions are short.

Glossary for a delta-normal VaR report: which definition of a VaR measure is fully correct?

question:
A risk analyst at a Singapore family office is preparing the VaR page of the quarterly board pack for a three-asset portfolio. The board pack uses a 95% confidence level ($\alpha=$ 1.65); the office’s separate regulatory return uses 99% ($\alpha=$ 2.33). Volatilities are for the reporting horizon.

| Asset | Position (SGD m) | Volatility (%) | Expected return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 18 | 7.5 |
| 2 | 5 | 7 | 3.0 |
| 3 | 3 | 22 | 9.0 |

Correlations: $\rho_{12} =$ 0.30, $\rho_{13} =$ 0.60, $\rho_{23} =$ 0.20.

The diversification benefit that should be reported in the board pack is closest to:

options.A: SGD 0.67 million
options.B: SGD 3.37 million
options.C: SGD 1.37 million

Three-asset SGD portfolio: diversification benefit at 95% for the board pack (99% figure is a distractor).

$\text{x}^{'}\Sigma\text{x} = \sum_{\text{i}} \text{x}^{2}_{\text{i}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{i}} +$ 2 $\sum_{\text{i}<\text{j}} \text{x}_{\text{i}} \text{x}_{\text{j}}\rho_{\text{ij}}\sigma_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{j}}$.

question: The CRO of a euro-denominated relative-value hedge fund presents the monthly risk report to the board. The fund is long EUR 400 million of corporate bonds (monthly volatility 2.0%) and short EUR 400 million of government bonds (monthly volatility 1.8%); the correlation between the two legs is 0.95. At 95% ($\alpha=$ 1.65) the report shows individual VaRs of EUR 13.20 million (long leg) and EUR 11.88 million (short leg), an undiversified VaR of EUR 25.08 million and a diversified VaR of EUR 4.17 million. A board member asks how the EUR 25.08 million figure should be read. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: It is the VaR the fund would face if the correlation between the legs rose to +1, so it is the worst case for the current positions.
options.B: It is the VaR at a correlation of −1; at a correlation of +1 the fund’s VaR would instead fall to zero, as each loss is offset by a matching gain.
options.C: It exceeds the diversified VaR by EUR 20.91 million, which is the amount of VaR that would be removed if the short leg were closed out.
options.D: It is the VaR the fund would face if the correlation fell to −1, so it is an absolute worst-case bound should correlations prove unstable.

solution:
Long/short EUR bond fund: how to read an undiversified VaR of EUR 25.08 million.

**Concept and theory**

For a long-only portfolio, undiversified VaR is the portfolio VaR at the worst correlation, which is +1: all losses arrive together. GARP stresses that “this interpretation differs when short sales are allowed”. With a long position in asset 1 and a short position in asset 2, Equation 5.12, rewritten with individual VaRs, becomes

$\text{VaR}_{\text{p}} = \sqrt{\text{VaR}^{2}_{1} + \text{VaR}^{2}_{2} + 2\rho_{12} \text{sign}(\text{x}_{1}\text{x}_{2}) \text{VaR}_{1}\text{VaR}_{2}}$,

question: A portfolio manager at a Japanese asset manager runs an equity overlay that is long JPY 10 billion of index A (annual volatility 20%) and short JPY 6 billion of index B (annual volatility 15%). The correlation between the returns of the two indices is 0.80. The manager reports annual VaR at 99% ($\alpha=$ 2.33). Which of the following correctly reports, for the short position in index B, its individual VaR and its component VaR?

options.A: Individual VaR −JPY 2.097 billion; component VaR −JPY 1.057 billion

question:
An internal auditor at a UK insurer is reviewing the section of the investment risk methodology that describes marginal VaR. The section makes four statements.

I. Marginal VaR is the partial derivative of portfolio VaR with respect to the currency position in a component, so it has no units.

II. Marginal VaR equals $\alpha\text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}})$/$\sigma_{\text{p}}$, which can also be written as (VaR/W$) \times\beta_{\text{i}}$, where $\beta_{\text{i}}$ is the slope from regressing $\text{R}_{\text{i}} \text{on R}_{\text{p}}$.

III. A long position always has a positive marginal VaR, because adding to it adds its own volatility to the portfolio.

IV. Marginal VaR cannot be produced until the portfolio has been revalued a second time with the position changed.

Which of these statements should the auditor accept as correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

solution:
UK insurer methodology audit: four statements about marginal VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Marginal VaR is “the change in portfolio VaR resulting from taking an additional dollar of exposure to a given component”, that is, “the partial (or linear) derivative with respect to the component position”. Because it is a ratio of currency amounts it is unitless. Its sign is the sign of cov$(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}})$: a component whose return moves against the portfolio has a negative marginal VaR, whatever the sign of the holding. question: A senior risk analyst at a US dealer bank supports a trading desk whose book holds about 120,000 trades; a full VaR run takes 12 minutes. A client proposes a trade whose exposures to two risk factors are each about 35% of the desk’s current exposure to those factors. The head of trading wants to quote within a minute and proposes to estimate the trade’s incremental VaR as $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \times$ a, using the marginal VaR vector from the last run. Which of the following comments by the analyst is most accurate?

options.A: The shortcut gives the exact incremental VaR for a trade of any size, because the marginal VaR vector is the derivative of VaR at the current positions.
options.B: The shortcut reuses the marginal VaR vector from the last run and trades accuracy for speed; it suits small trades, but a trade this large needs a before-and-after revaluation, as VaR changes nonlinearly.
options.C: The shortcut is most valuable for small books, because a full revaluation of a small book requires the largest number of computations.
options.D: The trade can be classed as a hedge without either method if its own individual VaR is smaller than the desk’s current portfolio VaR.

solution:
US dealer, 120,000 trades, 12-minute VaR run, large client trade: is the $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a shortcut appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP contrasts two ways to measure incremental VaR:

|  | Full revaluation | Marginal VaR shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | $\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{p}}$ | $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a |
| Inputs | A second VaR run with the trade | Marginal VaR vector, a by-product of the last run |
| Speed | Slow; operations grow with the square of the number of risk factors | Fast; allows real-time trading limits |
| Accuracy | Exact; captures the nonlinear response of VaR | First-order; good when the trade is small relative to the portfolio |

question: A junior risk analyst at a Chinese securities firm reviews a two-position book. Position 1 is CNY 50 million with annual volatility 16%; Position 2 is CNY 30 million with annual volatility 25%. The correlation between the two positions is 0.30, and the firm uses annual VaR at 95% ($\alpha=$ 1.65). The head of the desk is considering closing Position 2 entirely. Which of the following correctly gives the component VaR of Position 2 and the exact reduction in portfolio VaR if Position 2 is closed?

options.A: Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 7.425 million
options.B: Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 9.801 million
options.C: Component VaR CNY 12.375 million; exact reduction CNY 7.425 million
options.D: Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 8.250 million

Two-position CNY book: component VaR of Position 2 against the exact VaR reduction from closing it.

Component VaR, $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{x}_{\text{i}}$, takes the slope of VaR at the current holding and extends it linearly over the whole position. It therefore only approximates the effect of deleting the position; “the quality of this linear approximation improves when the VaR components are small”. The exact effect of deleting position i is an incremental VaR: the full portfolio VaR minus the VaR of the portfolio without i. In a two-asset book, the portfolio without position 2 is position 1 alone, whose VaR is its individual VaR. question:
A bank regulator reviewing a firm’s internal risk-decomposition framework reads four statements about component VaR in a delta-normal setting.

I. The component VaRs of all positions add up exactly to the diversified portfolio VaR, because the weighted sum of the betas, $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$, equals one.

II. A position’s component VaR equals its individual VaR multiplied by its correlation with the portfolio, so its absolute value cannot exceed its individual VaR.

III. Component VaR approximates the change in VaR from deleting a position most closely in portfolios made up of a few large positions.

IV. Expressing each position’s individual VaR as a share of the undiversified VaR gives the same percent contributions as component VaR, even when correlations are below one.

Which of these statements are correct?

options.A: I only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I and II only

solution:
Regulator review: four statements about component VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Three properties of component VaR matter here.

1. Additivity. $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR} \sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ VaR, because $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$ is the beta of the portfolio with itself, which is one (Equation 5.28).
2. Bound. $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{i}}\rho_{\text{i}}$ (Equation 5.29) and $|\rho_{\text{i}}| \le$ 1, so $|\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}}| \le\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$; Schweser: component VaR “will generally be less than” stand-alone VaR because of diversification.

question: A risk consultant engaged by a Dutch pension fund is presenting to newly hired analysts on why the fund’s risk system reports marginal VaR alongside individual (stand-alone) VaR when portfolio managers decide which positions to change. Which of the following statements made in the presentation is most accurate?

options.A: Ranking positions by individual VaR is sufficient to decide which position to trim, since the position with the highest stand-alone volatility always contributes most to portfolio risk.
options.B: Marginal VaR requires a separate full revaluation of the portfolio for each position, so it is mainly suited to overnight analysis rather than to decisions taken during the trading day.
options.C: Because portfolios are typically traded incrementally owing to transaction costs, the decision-relevant measure is how a small change in each position alters portfolio VaR, which is what marginal VaR captures.
options.D: Marginal VaR measures the change in portfolio VaR from deleting a position in its entirety, which makes it the preferred tool for deciding whether to liquidate a holding completely.

solution:
Risk consultant explains to new analysts why the risk system reports marginal VaR when managers decide which positions to change.

**Concept and theory**

A VaR number tells a manager how much the whole portfolio could lose; it does not by itself tell the manager what to do. GARP opens Section 5.2 with exactly that question: “Which position should I alter to modify my VaR most effectively?” Two facts make marginal VaR the answer.

First, individual VaRs are not sufficient. Volatility measures the uncertainty of an asset taken in isolation, but once the asset sits in a portfolio what matters is its contribution to portfolio risk, which depends on its covariance with the rest of the portfolio. loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese asset manager runs a JPY 50 billion multi-asset portfolio with a one-month 95% VaR of JPY 2.0 billion. She must reduce exactly one position by JPY 1 billion, with the proceeds held in riskless cash, and wants the largest reduction in portfolio VaR. The risk system reports:

| Position | Weight (%) | Annualized volatility (%) | Beta to portfolio |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 40 | 14 | 0.80 |
| Q | 25 | 22 | 1.10 |
| R | 20 | 18 | 1.35 |
| S | 15 | 10 | 0.90 |

Which position should she reduce, and what is the approximate reduction in portfolio VaR?

options.A: Position R; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 54 million.
options.B: Position Q; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 44 million.
options.C: Position R; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 540 million.
options.D: Position P; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 32 million.

solution:
JPY 50 billion portfolio, VaR JPY 2.0 billion; cut one position by JPY 1 billion using betas to the portfolio.

**Concept and theory**
